User guide

Everything you can do
with RackTrack.

Point your phone at a rack. RackTrack works out what is inside it — every slot, every device, every port — and checks it against your records. This guide walks through every job, one at a time, in the order you will meet them.

What RackTrack does

Read this first

RackTrack turns your phone into a rack survey tool. You take one photo of a rack. The app looks at that photo and works out what is inside the rack — every slot, every device, the make and model of each switch, how many ports it has, and which ports have cables in them. Then it compares all of that against your equipment records and tells you where the two do not agree.

One photo gives youMeaning
A slot mapEvery U position in the rack, numbered from the top down.
A device mapWhich slot holds a switch, a server, a patch panel, a firewall, a power strip — or nothing.
Switch identityThe make and model, read off the labels and logos in your photo.
A port layoutHow many ports, what kind (RJ45, SFP, SFP+, QSFP), and which ones are in use.
Firmware adviceThe newest version published for that model, and what changed in it.
A rack diagramThe rack drawn in 2D and 3D, with the cables between devices.
A records checkA comparison against your database, flagging anything that does not match.
note
You do not need any of the extra setup (switch passwords, a records database) to scan a rack and read the result. Those come from the photo alone. The extra setup only unlocks the live-network screens.

Work that used to take a clipboard, a torch and an hour of counting now takes about a minute.

What you are allowed to do

Everyone

RackTrack has four kinds of user. Which one you are decides which screens you can open, and whose scans you can see. If a screen in this guide is marked administrators only and you are not one, the app simply sends you back to the home screen — it does not show you an error.

You are aYou can
MemberScan racks and read the results. You see only your own scans. This is most people.
Site managerThe same as a member.
Organization adminAll of the above, plus: add sites, add and invite people, connect your records database, use the Marketplace, and see every scan in your company.
Platform ownerEverything, across every company — including approving new companies that sign up.

The first time you open RackTrack

Everyone

The first time you open the app, a short tour appears over the screen. It has four slides and takes about fifteen seconds.

The tour tells youIn short
Welcome to RackTrackTurn a photo of a rack into a labelled map of what is inside.
1 · Scan a rackPoint the camera at the rack (or upload a photo or short video) and press Scan.
2 · Review the resultsSee each device, where it sits, and its details. Tap any one to dig deeper or fix a label.
3 · Check the portsOpen the Ports tab to see the switch live — which ports are free, which are connected, and what is plugged in.
note
Click Skip at any point to dismiss it, or Start scanning on the last slide. It does not come back.
tip
The tour is a summary of exactly the three tasks this guide covers next. If you have read this far, you can safely skip it.

Create an account for a new company

If your company is new to RackTrack

Use this if nobody at your company uses RackTrack yet. You become the administrator. If a colleague has already invited you, skip this and read the next page instead.

Do this

  1. On the welcome screen, click Get Started.
  2. Fill in your Email, pick a Username, type your company's name in Organization, and choose a Password. You type the password twice.
  3. Look at the bar under the password. It tells you the one thing still missing — for example “Need a digit”. When it says “✓ Strong password”, and the second box says “✓ matches”, the Continue button turns on.
  4. Click Continue. RackTrack emails you a six-digit code.
  5. Type the code into the six boxes, then click Verify.
  6. You land on a waiting screen. Someone at RackTrack has to approve your new company before you can scan — see “Waiting for approval”.
warning
The code stops working after one minute. Have your email open before you click Continue. If it runs out, click Resend and use the new one straight away.
tip
Your password needs all five of these: 8 characters or more, one CAPITAL letter, one small letter, one number, and one symbol (like ! or @).

Join a company that invited you

If you got an invitation link

An administrator sends you a link. You are joining their company — you are not making a new one.

Do this

  1. Open the link they sent you. The page tells you what you are joining, for example “Join Acme · London as Member”.
  2. Your email address is already filled in and cannot be changed. That is on purpose — the invitation was made for that address.
  3. Pick a username, choose a password, and click Join.
  4. You are signed in and taken straight to the scan screen.
warning
An invitation link works only once, and it stops working after seven days. If yours has run out, ask for a new one. The old link cannot be made to work again.
note
RackTrack does not send the invitation email for your administrator — they copy the link and send it to you themselves. So it may reach you by chat, or from their own email address.

Sign in

Everyone

What you are looking at

Organization
Leave this empty. You only need it if your username exists at more than one company, which is rare.
Username or email
Either one works.
Password
The eye icon on the right shows what you typed, which helps when a phone keyboard is fighting you.
Forgot password?
Sends you a code by email. See the next page.

Do this

  1. Type your username (or your email) and your password.
  2. Click Sign in.
After signing in you land onIf you are
The Organizations screenAn administrator, or the platform owner
The scan screenEveryone else
tip
You stay signed in for 30 days. Losing phone signal does not sign you out — RackTrack is built to keep working in a datacenter with no reception.
note
If you see the words rate_limited on screen, it means you have tried to sign in too many times in one minute. Wait a minute, then try again.

You forgot your password

Everyone

Do this

  1. On the sign-in screen, click Forgot password? and type your email.
  2. RackTrack emails you a six-digit code. Type it in and press Verify code.
  3. Now you choose. Yes, change password lets you set a new one. No, take me to the app signs you in and leaves your old password alone.
tip
No, take me to the app is the quick way out when you have simply mistyped your password three times and you know it is right really.
warning
The code dies one minute after it was sent — including while you sit looking at the “Code verified” screen. Do not stop to make tea.

You are stuck on “Waiting for approval”

New companies

A brand-new company has to be approved before anyone in it can scan. The screen checks by itself every few seconds, and lets you in the moment you are approved. You do not need to sign in again, or refresh the page.

The screen saysIt meansDo this
Waiting for approvalNobody has looked at your request yet.Wait. The screen will let you in on its own.
Request not approvedYour request was turned down.Speak to whoever runs RackTrack. Nothing in the app will change this.
Organization deactivatedYour company has been switched off.Speak to whoever runs RackTrack. It comes back on its own if they switch you back on.
warning
Nobody is emailed when you sign up. The person who approves new companies only finds out by opening their own screen and looking. If you have been waiting a while, go and tell them.

Finding your way around

Everyone

A bar down the left side holds Home, Scan, Profile and — if you are an administrator — Marketplace.

What you are looking at

Home
The welcome screen.
Scan
Where you upload a photo of a rack.
Profile
Your account, and the list of every rack you have scanned.
Marketplace
Buying and selling gear. Administrators only.
warning
On an iPad there is no shutter button. The shutter is the middle button of the phone's bottom bar, and an iPad does not have that bar. So on an iPad, use Upload and pick a photo — or take the photo on a phone.
note
Those six rack links disappear if you refresh the page, and they are cleared on purpose when you start a new scan. To get back to a rack from last week, use Profile → Recent Scans instead.

Once you open a scanned rack, six more links appear for that rack: Overview, Ports, Topology, Network, Switches and Drift. Each one is a different way of looking at the same rack, and each has its own page in this guide.

Taking a photo the app can read

Everyone

How good your result is depends almost entirely on how good your photo is. So while you aim, the app watches the picture and tells you the one thing to fix. A box is drawn on screen to line the rack up in, and a line of text sits under it.

If the text saysIt meansSo do this
“Move closer so the rack fills the frame”The rack is too small in the picture.Step towards the rack until it fills the box.
“Move to better lighting”It is too dark, or a light behind the rack is blowing out the picture.Move, or turn slightly so the light is not behind the rack.
“Hold steady — keep still for focus”The picture is blurred.Tuck your elbows in and wait a second before pressing.
“Looks great — tap the shutter below”All three checks passed.Take the photo.
warning
The shutter will not fire until all three checks pass. So if pressing SCAN seems to do nothing at all, the app is not broken — read the line of text and fix what it is complaining about.

Four rules of thumb. Stand square to the rack, not off to one side — a side-on photo hides the ports. Hold the camera level with the middle of the rack, not up high or down low. Get the whole rack in, from the top rail to the bottom rail. And if cables hang over the front of the rack, take extra photos from the left and the right so the app can see behind the bundles.

Scan a rack

Everyone · this is the main job

What you are looking at

Upload / Camera
Choose whether to use a photo you already have, or take one now.
SINGLE / MULTI / VIDEO
SINGLE is one photo of one rack — the normal case. MULTI is for a rack too tall for one photo. VIDEO is for a whole row of racks.
The drop area
Press it to browse for a photo on your device.
Incident link (Optional)
Only appears if your company has connected ServiceNow. Leave it on Manual scan for ordinary work.
Analyze Rack
The button that starts everything. It stays greyed out until you have picked a photo.

Do this

  1. Open SCAN.
  2. Choose Camera to take a photo now, or Upload → SINGLE to use one you already have.
  3. If you are using the camera: line the rack up in the box until the text says “Looks great”, then take the photo (on a phone — see the warning on the previous page).
  4. Click Analyze Rack.
  5. Wait a few seconds. You land on the rack's Overview, which is the next page of this guide.
note
The progress bar is a guess, not a measurement. It runs up to about 88% and then waits there until the real work is done. A scan sitting at 88% for a few seconds is normal. It is not stuck.
tip
Photographing the same rack twice costs you nothing. RackTrack recognises that it is the same photo and hands you back the earlier result immediately — with any corrections you made still in place.

Scan a rack that is too tall for one photo

Everyone

Some racks are too tall to fit in one photo without standing so far back that the labels go unreadable. Take several photos instead, and let RackTrack join them together.

Do this

  1. Open SCAN → Upload → MULTI.
  2. Click Select photos and add between 2 and 8 photos of the rack.
  3. Click Stitch & Analyze.
tip
Make each photo overlap the next one by about a third. The app joins them by finding the bits that appear in both, so it needs some shared detail to work with. You do not have to add them in order — the app works the order out.
note
This is for one tall rack. To capture a row of separate racks, use a video instead — that is the next page.

Scan a whole row of racks at once

Everyone

Record one video as you walk along the row. RackTrack finds each rack in the video, picks the best frame for each one, and analyses them one by one. Each rack gets its own full result.

Do this

  1. Open SCAN → Upload → VIDEO.
  2. Upload a video panning steadily across the row. It must be between 1 and 120 seconds long.
  3. Click Analyze Rack.
  4. You land on the first rack. A strip of rack buttons now runs across the top — one per rack.
warning
Linking a ticket turns this off. A ticket is about one specific rack, so if you pick an incident, RackTrack analyses only that rack — even from a video.

Click any rack in that strip to jump to it. You stay on the same kind of page as you move: if you are looking at Ports for rack 1, you land on Ports for rack 2. The Combined 3D button draws every rack in the row in one picture, so you can see the links between them.

The app refused your photo

Everyone

When a photo is too small, too blurred, tilted, or buried under cables, RackTrack stops and offers you two buttons: Retake and Proceed anyway.

The messageWhat it really meansWhat to do
“Please take the photo from the front of the rack…”The app found no devices at all. Usually the photo is side-on, or very dark.Stand square to the rack and take it again.
“Please upload a clearer photo of the rack…”It could read fewer than three slots.Get the whole rack in the picture and hold still.
“The image appears tilted…”The camera was rotated.Hold the phone straight and retake.
“This rack is heavily covered by cables…”Cable bundles are hiding the equipment.Take extra photos from the left and the right of the rack.
“Camera access denied…”Your phone is blocking the camera.Allow the camera in your settings, or use Upload instead.
warning
Proceed anyway turns the safety checks off. The app will then analyse the photo however bad it is — and a bad photo comes back with devices missing, or with an empty rack. Taking the photo again is nearly always faster than untangling a wrong result. Use Retake unless you have a reason not to.

The rack overview

Everyone

Every scan lands here. Your photo comes back with a box drawn round each device, and a name on each box. This is the screen you will spend the most time on.

What you are looking at

The photo
Your own photo, with a coloured box around every device the app recognised.
The name on each box
Read off the label in the photo where the app could read one — otherwise made up from the slot number, like U12-SW01.
Device list
The same devices as a dropdown. Picking one here is the same as tapping its box.
Zoom buttons
Get closer. You can also pinch, or scroll.
ANALYZED badge
Confirms the scan finished.

Do this

  1. Click a box to pick that device.
  2. Click it again to zoom right into it and hide everything else. Back to rack brings you out.
  3. Pinch or scroll to get closer. Once zoomed in, drag to move around.
note
Empty slots, blanking plates, and anything the app could not identify are deliberately left unboxed. That is not a failure — it keeps the picture readable.

Find one particular port

Everyone · the job you came to do

This is the reason the app exists. You have been given a port number, and you need to put your finger on that exact port, in a rack of identical-looking switches, in a dark aisle.

Do this

  1. Pick the device from the Device list — or just tap it in the photo.
  2. Pick the kind of port: RJ45, SFP, Console or USB. Only the kinds that device actually has are shown, and each one tells you how many there are.
  3. Type the port number.
  4. Click Find Port.
It tells youWhich means
StatusConnected — there is a cable in it. Empty — there is not. Unknown — it could not tell.
Cable and ColorWhat kind of cable, and what colour it is. The colour is genuinely useful when you are following a cable by eye.
Linked endpointWhat is on the far end of the cable. This is marked LIVE, because the app asked the switch — it did not read it from the photo.
note
When the app is not sure, it says so, in as many words: “Not fully sure about this cable (42% confidence) — the photo resolution may be too low to read it clearly.” Believe your own eyes over the app when it hedges like that — and then correct it, which is the next page.

The app zooms your photo to that exact port and dims everything else, so there is no counting along a row in the dark. Click the picture to cycle between the whole rack, the device, and a close-up of the port.

Tell the app when it got something wrong

Everyone

RackTrack asks you to check its work. It asks in plain words — “Port 7 on Switch. Right?” — with a Yes and a No button. Saying No fixes your result on the spot.

It asksSay No whenThen
Port N on <device>. Right?The highlight landed on the wrong port.Type the port it really is. The app renumbers the device and moves the highlight.
Cable color is <colour>. Right?The colour is wrong.Pick the real colour from twelve swatches.
Detected as <type>. Right?It called a firewall a switch, or similar.Choose what it really is from a list.
Detected N ports. Right?The number of ports is wrong.Type the real number. The app counts them again and redraws them.
tip
These questions are worth the ten seconds they cost. Your answer fixes your result immediately, and it is also fed back into training, so the app gets better at your kit over time.
note
Correcting a port number does not change the number you asked for. If you tell the app “port 7 is really port 5”, it learns that the whole row is shifted, and then shows you where port 7 truly is.

Send a report, or talk to the switch

Everyone

Once a port is found, a row of buttons appears under it.

ButtonWhat it does
ViewShows the full report without leaving the page.
ReportOpens the report in a new tab, ready to save or print.
ShareSends it by Teams, Outlook or Slack. Your address is remembered for next time.
ConsoleOpens a direct connection to the switch, already pointed at this port.
FindLook up another port on the same device.
Change DeviceGo back to the device list.
New ScanStart again with a new rack.

The Console is worth knowing about. Instead of expecting you to remember switch commands, it gives you a menu of questions — pick one and it runs. When you press Done, it gathers everything it learned into a short report with a plain-English verdict at the top, such as “Link is DOWN — no device connected (or cable unplugged at the far end).”

Add the rack to your records

Only if your company connected a database

If your company has connected its equipment database, RackTrack checks every scan against it. When it finds a rack your records have never heard of, it offers to fill in the paperwork for you.

Do this

  1. Shortly after the scan, a message appears: “Rack not registered in CMDB”. Click Raise Ticket.
  2. RackTrack raises a request describing everything it found, and shows you the reference number. Write it down if you need it.
  3. Click Approve to write the equipment into your records.
  4. Successfully registered appears, listing every device, port and cable that was added.
note
The offer appears once, on a fresh scan, and only for about half a minute. If you click Not now it will not pester you again — but the rack stays unregistered.
warning
If your company has not connected a database, none of this ever appears. Your scan still works perfectly — you just do not get the records check.

Start a scan from an incident

Needs ServiceNow connected

If your company has connected ServiceNow, RackTrack pulls in your open incidents and lists them on the scan screen. Linking your scan to a ticket changes what the app does for you: instead of making you hunt for the port, it takes you straight to the one the ticket is about.

What you are looking at

Incident link (Optional)
The picker. It only appears when ServiceNow is connected and you have open tickets.
Manual scan
The default. No ticket — you pick the device and port yourself after the rack is analysed. This is ordinary work.
A ticket row
The incident number, then the device and port the ticket is about (SW-U22:Gi1/0/17), then how urgent it is. The line underneath is the ticket's own description.

Do this

  1. Open SCAN.
  2. Click the Incident link (Optional) box.
  3. Pick the ticket you are working on. Leave it on Manual scan if you are not working a ticket.
  4. Take or upload your photo as normal, then click Analyze Rack.
note
RackTrack checks you are at the right rack first. Before it analyses anything you will see “Verifying rack identity…”. It reads the labels in your photo and compares them with the rack the ticket points at.
warning
If you are at the wrong rack, it stops you. A Wrong rack message appears — “This isn't <rack name>” — showing what it read on your photo beside what it expected. That is the app saving you from working on the wrong equipment. Go and find the right rack.

The port is found for you

Needs ServiceNow connected

When a scan is linked to a ticket, RackTrack skips the device list entirely and jumps straight to the port named in the incident. You do not pick anything.

What you are looking at

Auto-targeted from INC…
Confirms which ticket this came from, with its description and the rack, device, port and management address.
Live · every 5s
RackTrack keeps watching that port while you work. It checks the switch every five seconds and shows whether the link is active or idle, what is on the far end, and how many devices are talking through it.
Cable attached — port is now active
The banner that appears the moment the port comes alive. This is your proof the fix worked.

Do this

  1. Take the photo. RackTrack analyses it and lands you straight on the target port.
  2. Do the physical work — plug the cable in, or swap it.
  3. Watch the live strip. When the port comes up, the app tells you, with the time it happened.
tip
You do not have to keep re-checking the switch. The port is watched for you while you are standing there. When it goes live, the banner says so — and notes that the incident is likely resolved.
note
The “Right?” correction questions are hidden in ticket mode. The device and port came from your records, not from a guess, so there is nothing to correct.

Send the work note back to ServiceNow

Needs ServiceNow connected

RackTrack writes up what it found and can post it to the incident for you — so the ticket gets a proper record without you typing it out on your phone in a cold aisle.

What you are looking at

Agent Analysis
A short plain-English summary of what the app thinks is going on, with a confidence score.
Show details
Opens the evidence: the signals it used, its reasoning, and a preview of the work note before anything is sent.
Copy note
Copies the note to your clipboard, so you can paste it wherever you like.
Post to ServiceNow
Writes the note onto the incident.

Do this

  1. Read the summary at the top. That is the app's answer.
  2. Click Show details and read the work-note preview. Check it before you send it.
  3. Click Post to ServiceNow — or Copy note if you would rather paste it in yourself.
Afterwards you may seeIt means
Posted to ServiceNowDone. The note is on the incident.
Skipped — low confidenceThe app was not sure enough to post by itself. Read it, and if you agree, use Force post.
Already posted — no changeNothing new to add since last time.
Rate-limited — already posted within 24hA note went on this incident today already.
warning
Read the note before you post it. It goes onto a real ticket that other people will read and act on. The app is confident, not infallible.
tip
If the scan finds that the rack does not match your records — the wrong device in the slot the ticket names — RackTrack shows Physical Drift Detected, with what your records expect beside what it actually saw, and a Raise ticket button to report it.

See what is plugged in right now

Needs the switch password saved

Every other screen in this guide is built from your photo. This one is not. This screen logs into the switch over the network and asks it directly: what is plugged in, what is talking, and what is free. So it tells you what is true this second, not what was true when the photo was taken.

What you are looking at

The switch name and live dot
Which switch you are looking at, and confirmation it answered.
FIRMWARE · UPTIME · MGMT IP · MAC · POE DRAW
The switch's own details, read from the switch.
IN USE
Ports with something plugged in and working, out of the total.
AVAILABLE
Ports you could actually plug into today.
IDENTIFIED
Ports where the thing on the far end announced itself, so the app knows what it is.
FACEPLATE
A map of the real front of the switch — a port shown here sits where that port sits on the metal. Green is working, amber is an uplink carrying lots of devices, grey is free.
All · In Use · Available · Linked · Errors
Filters for the list underneath.
POE · POWERED
Which ports are powering a device through the network cable, and how many watts.
warning
A port that looks free but says “Reserved” has a name written on it. Somebody labelled it on the switch, which usually means it is spoken for. Ask before you take it.
note
This screen can fail even when your scan worked perfectly — if the switch is not reachable, or its password is not saved on the server. That is a network problem, not a scanning problem. The messages are explained under When something goes wrong.

See what is on the end of each cable

Needs the switch password saved

Do this

  1. Open Ports and choose the Cables tab.
  2. Click any row. It opens up to show both ends of that cable.
  3. Where one port feeds a whole downstream network, the app lists every device behind it, and tells you who made each one.
warning
RackTrack can only see what the switch can see. A patch panel, or a wall socket, in the middle of a cable run has no electronics in it — so the switch cannot see it, and neither can the app. The cable looks like it runs straight from the switch to the far end. That is how the physics works; it is not a missing feature.

Check whether the switch can reach something

Needs the switch password saved

This asks the switch to try to reach an address. That is the whole point of it: it tests the path your equipment takes, not the path your laptop takes over the office wifi. The two are often different, and that difference is often the bug you are hunting.

Do this

  1. Open Ports → Ping.
  2. Type where you want to test to — an IP address, or a name.
  3. Click Ping. RackTrack pings it from the switch and shows you the reply.
tip
The Quick ping buttons save typing. 8.8.8.8 checks the whole path out to the internet. The gateway button checks only the first hop out of your rack. If the gateway answers but 8.8.8.8 does not, you have just proved the problem is not in your rack — which is usually the thing you needed to know.
note
There is no traceroute here, on purpose. Traceroute needs a higher level of access to the switch than RackTrack asks for. RackTrack signs in with a read-only account, which is safer — it cannot change anything on your switch — and ping works fine at that level.

Check whether a switch's firmware is current

Everyone

For each switch the app found in your photo, it can look up the newest firmware the maker has published, and show you what changed in it — so you can decide whether the upgrade is worth doing.

Do this

  1. Open the rack → Switches, and pick the switch's tab.
  2. If the card says Not detected, the label was unreadable in your photo. Click Enter make / model and type them in — the lookup needs both to work.
  3. Open the Firmware tab. If no version is shown, click Enter version and type in what the switch is running.
  4. Read the coloured pill: it tells you in three words whether you need to act.
It showsWhich means
CurrentThe version you are running.
LatestThe newest version RackTrack could actually confirm from the maker.
Min safeThe oldest version the maker still considers acceptable, when they publish one. Upgrade at least this far.
Release notes ↗The maker's own list of what changed. Read this before you upgrade.
warning
“Latest version unknown” does not mean you are up to date. It means the app could not confirm what the newest version is. Follow the Check site ↗ link and look for yourself before you relax.
warning
Anything you type in here is saved in this browser only. It does not reach the server, your records database, or your colleagues, and it is gone if you clear your browser or pick up a different phone. Treat it as a note to yourself.

Choose the right SFP module

Everyone

An SFP is the little plug-in module that lets a switch take a fibre cable. Which ones fit depends on the switch. Given the empty slots on your switch, this screen suggests modules that fit, with a price and a link to buy.

warning
Check the suggestion against your switch's own compatibility list before you spend money. When RackTrack cannot get a definite answer for your exact model, it falls back to a general catalogue, which may not be the right brand for your switch.

It also suggests direct-attach cables. These have the modules built into both ends, so for a short run inside one rack they replace the module-and-fibre pair completely — and they are usually cheaper.

See the rack as a diagram

Everyone

2D draws the rack as a tall column of numbered slots — the same view as the drawing on the cabinet door. 3D puts the same rack in space: drag to spin it around, scroll to zoom.

Do this

  1. Click any device. The panel underneath fills in with its details.
  2. Peer chips show what it is connected to. 2× means two cables run to that neighbour.
  3. The Ports table lists every port: whether it is connected, which cable is in it, and what is on the other end.
ColourMeaning
GreenA connected network (copper) port.
CyanAn SFP (fibre) port.
AmberAn uplink — the cable carrying traffic out of this rack.
GreyFree.
note
The diagram is drawn in the background after a scan, so it can lag a few seconds behind. If you see “Topology is being prepared”, wait a moment and click Retry.

See what the network says about the rack

Needs a Netdisco server

Your scan tells you what is physically in the rack. This screen tells you what is electrically alive in it: which ports are genuinely up this second, which network each one is on, and how many machines are talking through each.

What you are looking at

Network View online
Confirms the discovery server answered. If it says offline, nothing below will fill in.
5 live
How many of the devices in your scan the network actually recognised.
A device row with an IP
You can click it to open its ports.
not in Network View
The network has no record of this device. These rows are greyed out and cannot be opened.
The bar on the right
How many of that device's ports are up, out of the total.

Do this

  1. Open the rack → Network.
  2. Check the pill in the corner says Network View online.
  3. Click a device that shows an IP address.
  4. Filter its ports with Live, Up, Down or All.
note
Patch panels never appear here, and that is correct. A patch panel has no electronics in it, so it cannot announce itself to the network. Its absence is expected.
warning
This screen needs a Netdisco server, set up by an administrator. Without one, the page says “Network view is being prepared” for ever. That message means “nobody has set this up”, not “try again in a minute”.

Find out what changed, and when

Needs a monitored switch

RackTrack can log into a switch once a minute, every minute, and write down the state of every port. This screen shows you the result. Drift is the word for what changed — the gap between how the rack was left and how it is now.

What you are looking at

Streaming
Confirms the app is polling this switch.
The grid of ports
One box per port. A green line underneath means the link is up, red means down.
SPECS
What the port is doing right now — speed, duplex, what is plugged in.
TIMELINE
A chart of the last hour, day or week. This is how you spot a port that has been flapping on and off.
HISTORY
A list, in plain English, of everything that has changed on this port.

Do this

  1. Open Drift. The switch appears at the top, marked Streaming.
  2. Click the port you care about.
  3. Open the HISTORY tab and read the list of changes.
  4. Open the TIMELINE tab and widen the Window to a day or a week. This is how you tell a one-off outage from a port that has been failing on and off for a fortnight.
  5. Press the round Poll now button to check the switch immediately, instead of waiting for the next minute.
The history saysWhich usually means
Link went down / came upSomething was plugged in, unplugged, or it failed.
Port administratively disabledA person, or a script, switched the port off. This was deliberate.
Speed changed 1 Gbps → 100 MbpsThe port negotiated down. Very often a damaged cable, or a dying fibre module.
LLDP neighbor changed: X → YThe important one. The cable now goes to a different machine than it used to. Somebody re-patched it.
tip
A quiet LLDP neighbor changed is the classic cause of “but it worked yesterday”. When a service breaks overnight and nobody admits to touching anything, look here first — the switch remembers even when people do not.
warning
This must be set up on the server by an administrator, and today it works with TP-Link switches. If the screen says “Waiting for first poll…” and never changes, it means no switch is being watched.

Look up a datasheet

Everyone · no scan needed

You do not need a scan, or the equipment in front of you. Type a make and a model and get the datasheet.

Do this

  1. Open Specifications.
  2. Type the Make / Vendor and the Model.
  3. Click Get specifications.
tip
Pick the maker from the list that drops down as you type, rather than typing it out yourself. That way the name is guaranteed to match the one the app searches under.

You get the port count, the throughput, the power draw, the PoE budget and the physical size, with a link to the maker's page.

Check any firmware version

Everyone · no scan needed

You do not need a scan, or the switch in front of you. Type in what you are running and find out whether there is something newer.

Do this

  1. Open Firmware Check.
  2. Type the make, the model, and the version you are running.
  3. Click Check firmware.

You get a single plain sentence as the answer — “You're up to date.”, “An upgrade is available.”, or “We couldn't confirm the latest version.” The release notes, which tell you what actually changed, sit behind Show details.

Open a rack you scanned earlier

Everyone

Profile holds your account details — and, the reason you will actually open it, the list of every rack you have ever scanned.

Do this

  1. Open Profile.
  2. Scroll down to Recent Scans. Every rack is here, newest first, with its ID, how many devices and slots it found, and how long ago it was.
  3. Click any one to open the whole result again, exactly as it was. Show all shows the older ones.
tip
This is how you get back to a rack from last week. The rack links in the menu only remember the rack you are on right now, and they are wiped when you start a new scan.
note
You see your own scans. Administrators see everyone's.

Connect your equipment database

Administrators only

This is how you tell RackTrack where your equipment records live, so it can compare what it sees in a rack against what you believe is in that rack.

Do this

  1. Go to Profile → Integrations, or open Connections.
  2. Click + Add connection.
  3. Give it a Name you will recognise, choose the Type, and fill in the login details.
  4. Click Save & use.
SystemWhat you need to have ready
ServiceNow / CMDBYour instance ID — just the bit before .service-now.com — plus a username and a password.
NetBoxThe web address, and an API token from your NetBox profile.
SolarWinds OrionThe server address, a username and a password.
CA / DX SpectrumThe web address, a username and a password.
Your own SQL databaseA PostgreSQL or MySQL connection string.
Your own REST APIA web address, and a token if it needs one.
note
There is no “Test connection” button — saving is the test. Watch the message that appears afterwards. If the details are wrong, that is where it will tell you.
warning
Only one connection is switched on at a time, and every screen in the app reads from that one. Switching it changes where all your data comes from. RackTrack does not blend two systems together.
note
Passwords are stored scrambled and are never shown again, not even to you. So when you edit a connection, the password boxes open empty. Leave them empty to keep the saved password; type in them only to replace it.

Add people to your team

Administrators only

A company contains sites (your buildings), and each site contains people. A scan belongs to the site of whoever took it.

Do this

  1. Find the site in the list and click Invite.
  2. Type their email and choose their Role.
  3. Click Create invite link, then click Copy.
  4. Send them the link yourself — by email, or chat, or however you like.
Two ways to add someoneHow it worksUse it when
InviteRackTrack makes a link. They open it and choose their own username and password.The normal way. Nobody has to share a password.
+ Add memberYou choose their username and password, and hand them over.A shared account, a contractor, or someone with no email you can reach.
warning
RackTrack does not send the invitation for you. If you do not copy the link and send it, nothing ever reaches them. The link works once, and it stops working after seven days.
tip
Click any person to filter the scan list to just their work. Click a site to filter to that site. It is the quickest way to see who has actually been out surveying.

Approve a new company

The platform owner only

When a company signs up, it appears under Pending approvals, and nobody in it can use the app until you act.

ButtonWhat happens
ApproveThey are let in immediately — their waiting screen opens by itself.
RejectThey are told the request was turned down. Their account still exists.
RemoveThe company, and all its people, sites and invitations, are deleted for good.
warning
Remove cannot be undone. Reject is the one you can change your mind about. Use Reject unless you are certain.
note
You are not emailed when a company signs up. You only find out by opening this screen and looking, so it is worth checking it regularly — somebody may be sitting on the waiting screen right now.

Sell gear you no longer need

Administrators only

Do this

  1. Open Marketplace and click + Sell something.
  2. Type the Vendor and Model — the title fills itself in, and you can edit it.
  3. Choose a Category and a Condition.
  4. Set a Price, or leave it blank so buyers see Make an offer.
  5. Upload a photo (JPG, PNG or WebP, up to 8 MB) and wait for Photo ready.
  6. Click Publish listing.
note
There is no checkout and no messaging inside RackTrack. A buyer contacts you through your RackTrack username, and you agree the price and the shipping between yourselves.
tip
Use Post a want for kit you are looking for. Colleagues sitting on a rack of decommissioned gear can then find you.

You cannot get in

Everyone
What you seeWhyWhat to do
Stuck on Waiting for approvalYour company has not been approved.Go and tell whoever runs RackTrack. They are not emailed about it.
The word rate_limitedToo many tries in one minute.Wait a minute, then try again.
“This account has been deactivated.”An administrator switched your account off.Speak to your administrator.
The six-digit code does not workIt expired. Codes last one minute.Click Resend and use the new one straight away.
Your invitation link failsIt has been used already, or it is more than seven days old.Ask for a fresh invitation. The old one cannot be revived.

The scan is not working

Everyone
What you seeWhyWhat to do
Pressing SCAN does not take the photoThe three quality checks have not all passed yet.Read the line of text under the box, and fix the one thing it names.
No shutter button at allYou are on an iPad or a computer. The shutter is the phone's bottom SCAN button, which does not exist there.Use Upload, or take the photo on a phone.
Devices are missing from the resultThe photo was taken at an angle, or cables are hiding them.Retake it square-on, and add photos from the left and right.
The rack came back emptyA bad photo was pushed through with Proceed anyway.Scan it again properly, and let the checks do their job.
Progress sits at 88%Nothing is wrong. The bar is a guess, not a measurement.Wait.

The live switch screens are not working

Everyone

Remember that these screens talk to the switch over the network. They can fail even when your scan was perfect.

What you seeWhyWhat to do
“The switch didn't respond”You are not on the same network as the switch.Get off the guest wifi and onto the right network.
“Lost the SSH session”Most switches allow only one connection at a time, and somebody else has it.Click Retry in a moment.
“The switch rejected the saved credentials”The saved password is wrong or has changed.An administrator needs to save the new one.
Network view never loadsNo discovery server has been set up.Ask an administrator. It will never load until one exists.
Drift says “Waiting for first poll…” for everNo switch is being watched.Ask an administrator to set one up.

The information looks wrong

Everyone
What you seeWhyWhat to do
A switch says Not detectedThe label could not be read in the photo.Type the make and model in yourself.
“Latest version unknown”The app could not confirm the newest firmware. This is not the same as “you are up to date”.Follow the Check site ↗ link and check the maker's site.
A cable seems to skip a patch panelPatch panels have no electronics, so the switch cannot see them. Physics, not a bug.Nothing to fix.
The make and model you typed have vanishedThey were saved in that browser only.Type them again. They do not follow you to another phone.

Which screens need setting up

Everyone

Some screens read your photo. Some talk to the live network. One is a demonstration with made-up data. Knowing which is which will stop you acting on the wrong thing.

ScreenWhere its information comes fromNeeds setting up?
Scan · Overview · Find a portYour photo.No
Topology · 3DYour photo — the devices and cables it found.No
Switches · Firmware · SpecificationsYour photo for the model, then the maker's public website.No
PortsThe switch itself, right now, over the network.Yes — the switch password
DriftThe switch itself, checked once a minute.Yes — a watched switch (TP-Link today)
Network viewA Netdisco discovery server.Yes — a Netdisco server
Adding a rack to your recordsYour equipment database.Yes — a connected database
Working from a ticketYour ServiceNow incidents, pulled in live.Yes — ServiceNow connected
MarketplaceRackTrack's own records. These are real listings.No
The demo rack mapA demonstration. The racks, devices and addresses on that page are invented to show what a whole-estate view would look like.No — but it is not your data

Words explained

Everyone
WordWhat it means
U, or rack unitThe standard slot height in a rack. A 42U rack has 42 slots.
CMDBYour official list of what equipment you own and where it is.
DriftThe gap between what your records say and what is really there — or what has changed on a port since last time.
LLDPThe way a device shouts its own name to its neighbours. It is how RackTrack knows what is on the far end of a cable.
MAC addressThe unique serial number of a network card. Seeing one on a port means something alive is plugged into it.
SFP, SFP+, QSFPSlots that take a small plug-in module, usually for fibre. SFP+ is 10 gigabit; QSFP is faster still.
DACA cable with the modules already built into both ends. Cheaper than buying modules and fibre separately, for short runs.
PoEPower over Ethernet — the switch powering a device down the same cable that carries its data. It is how cameras and wifi points get their electricity.
VLANA separate network living on the same switch. Two machines on one switch but different VLANs cannot talk to each other directly.
UplinkThe port that carries traffic out of this switch to the rest of the network.
PingThe simplest network test there is: “are you there?”. RackTrack runs it from the switch, so it proves what the switch can reach — not what your laptop can.
Read-only accountThe kind of login RackTrack uses on your switch. It can look at things but cannot change them, which is why it is safe to give it.
